clinical_category: Peripheral nerve block - protection of numb or weak extremity
blueprint_topic: Regional analgesia safety teaching and prevention of injury
stem: After orthopedic surgery, a client has temporary numbness and weakness in one leg from a peripheral nerve block. Which teaching by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Do not stand, walk, or put pressure on the affected leg until the care team confirms it is safe; protect the numb limb until sensation and motor control return.
options.B: Bear full weight immediately because absence of pain confirms that the leg can safely support you.
options.C: Apply sustained pressure to the numb area to test whether sensation is returning, even if you cannot feel the pressure.
options.D: Remove prescribed protective devices because nerve-block numbness prevents pressure or fall injuries.

rationale: A is correct. ASRA Pain Medicine patient guidance explains that regional analgesia can produce temporary numbness, heaviness, weakness, and incomplete muscle control. Patients are instructed to check with the physician or nurse before using an affected extremity for standing or other motor tasks and not to put pressure on an extremity that remains numb. This reduces fall and pressure-injury risk while protective sensation and motor control are impaired. B incorrectly treats pain absence as proof of safe weight-bearing. C can expose an insensate limb to injury. D removes protection precisely when sensory or motor impairment may make injury harder to recognize. The final item uses observable safety actions rather than merely stating that a numb limb should be 'protected.'
educational_objective: Protect an extremity affected by a peripheral nerve block by avoiding unapproved weight-bearing or pressure and maintaining injury precautions until sensation and motor control have adequately returned.
source_organization: American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine (ASRA Pain Medicine)
source_document_title: Pain Relief After Surgery — Regional Anesthesia Patient Information
source_version_date: Current ASRA Pain Medicine patient-information resource accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: ASRA Patient Information → Regional Anesthesia → 'Pain relief after surgery' → Question 4: local anesthetics may cause numbness/heaviness, weight-bearing difficulty and fall risk. Question 6 'What will I feel after the block takes effect?': temporary numbness/heaviness/weakness and reduced muscle control; check with physician/nurse before standing or other motor tasks; do not put pressure on an extremity that feels numb.
source_claim_supported: Current ASRA guidance directly supports temporary sensory/motor impairment after regional blocks, caution with weight-bearing and motor tasks, fall prevention, and avoidance of pressure on a numb extremity.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p. 12 (PDF pageno 15): provide care related to parenteral therapies, evaluate client response and educate clients about treatment safety.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's generic ASA citation using exact ASRA regional-anesthesia patient guidance. The final item specifies the concrete safety behaviors directly supported by the source—avoid unapproved standing/weight-bearing and pressure on a numb extremity—while replacing weak distractors with realistic injury-risk errors.
audit_findings: The original safety idea was clinically sound but used a generic ASA homepage and did not provide an exact patient-instruction locator.
Fresh ASRA review directly instructs patients with numb/weak blocked extremities to check before standing or motor use and to avoid pressure on numb areas.
The final stem contains actual numbness and weakness so the precautions are directly tied to observed impairment rather than generalized to every regional block after effects have resolved.
Distractors test premature weight-bearing, pressure testing of insensate tissue and removal of protection; none is defensible.
